newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada board recommends sweeping pipeline changes.
newsitem.headline: Canada board recommends sweeping pipeline changes.

text.p: Canada's National Energy Board realeased its long-awaited report on oil and gas pipeline stress corrosion cracking (SCC) on Thursday, recommending sweeping changes to the way companies deal with the problem which has caused numerous ruptures.

The report of the NEB inquiry panel contained 27 recommendations for the problem that has been called a threat to public safety, including the implementation by all pipeline companies of a comprehensive SCC management program, improved emergency response practices, stepped-up research and information sharing.
"SCC remains a serious concern for the pipeline industry and for us as regulators," the inquiry's report said.
"Since SCC is a time-dependent process, without proper attention, it will worsen and be the cause of more pipeline failures."

The panel said SCC was responsible for 22 failures, including 12 ruptures on Canadian pipelines. Most of the SCC-related failures occurred since 1985 on pipelines coated with polyethylene tape and installed between 1968 and 1973, it said.
The NEB said it accepted the inquiry panel's conclusions and recommendations and would announce in the near future what steps it would take to implement them.
Concern about SCC on the TransCanada PipeLines Ltd system led to a board inquiry in 1993, but Canada's energy regulator concluded that SCC was being managed appropriately.
But, after two major ruptures and failures on the TransCanada system itwo years later, and more evidence of the widespread nature of the problem, the NEB launched the public inquiry.
The extensive probe went beyond Canada's SCC problem to draw on experience and expertise from other countries, the panel said, adding that conclusions would be of use outside Canada.

Amid industry concern, the panel examined whether reducing pipeline operating pressure would be effective in dealing with SCC. But the report said there was no clear evidence of a threshold pressure level below which SCC would not start and grow.
Also, mandated reductions in pressure would not prevent failures and would be very costly, it said.

"We find that there are other measures which are more systematic, efficient and effective in mitigating SCC and thereby promoting public safety," the report said. "Therefore, we believe that a general reduction in pressure would not be a logical or effective response to the SCC problem."
However, the report said pressure reductions "should be considered as a temporary measure for sections of a pipeline system where there is a threat of imminent failure."

Stress corrosion cracking starts when small cracks develop on the outside surface of the buried pipe. The cracks, at first, are not visible to the eye and are found in "colonies" with all cracks positioned in the same direction.
Over a number of years, the individual cracks may lengthen and deepen and the cracks within a colony may join together to form longer ones, which can result in ruptures.
